# Building B — seismic diaphragm shears and shear wall loads

You are the delegated design engineer for the lateral load path of **Building B** at the
Continental Divide Data Center in Lewis and Clark County, Montana. The shell is erected: the
precast wall panels are up, the roof deck is laid, and the Engineer of Record has issued the
project documents to you in `project/`, with the published standards available on this project in
`library/`.

Building B is a one-storey box. The exterior walls are 8 in solid normal-weight precast concrete
panels that span vertically from the foundation to the roof and cantilever above it to the top of
the parapet; they are the only seismic force-resisting elements. The roof is a bare steel deck
diaphragm on open-web joists, pierced by a mechanical well and a skylight band, and it carries six
roof-top units.

**The Engineer of Record has not selected the precast shear wall system, the deck attachment, the
chords and collectors, the panel connections or the anchorage. That is your scope.** Design it,
analyse it, and hand over the package below.

## What you are asked to produce

Write these five files, then zip them (no enclosing folder) to `output/submission.zip`:

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `design_record.json` | the machine-readable design and the quantities you report |
| `diaphragm_plan.dxf` | the plan drawings for the delegated design engineer |
| `seismic_calculations.xlsx` | the calculation package |
| `constraint_register.xlsx` | the requirements you applied, with their sources |
| `design_basis.md` | the design basis narrative |

Templates for all five, with the exact keys, sheet names and layer names, are in `templates/`.
Start from them. **Write a first complete version of all five files early — within roughly your
first 100 steps — and improve it afterwards; a package that is never written scores zero.**

### `diaphragm_plan.dxf`

Two plan views of the roof, one for **E-W** loading and one for **N-S** loading, in feet, showing
for each direction:

* the **seismic roof diaphragm shear** — the distributed diaphragm force `w_px` in **plf** along
  the building, and the design unit shear in each deck attachment zone;
* the **applied shear wall load `F_x` in kips** on each of the four exterior wall lines;
* the chord, collector and drag strut runs with their design axial forces;
* the deck attachment zone boundaries with the pattern assigned to each zone;
* a revision block, and a statement of whether the package is ASD or LRFD.

Required layers: `DIAPHRAGM_SHEAR`, `WALL_FORCE`, `CHORD`, `COLLECTOR`, `DECK_ZONE`, `GRID`,
`TITLE`.

### `seismic_calculations.xlsx`

Sheets `WEIGHTS`, `BASE_SHEAR`, `DIAPHRAGM_FORCES`, `WALL_FORCES`, `PARAPET_ANCHORAGE`,
`CHORD_FORCES`, covering the effective seismic weight, the seismic response coefficient, the
vertical distribution, the diaphragm design forces, the transfer of the inertia of the wall
cantilevering above the deck, the chord forces, and the force on every wall line for every design
case the criteria list.

### `constraint_register.xlsx`

One row per requirement you applied: the **document**, the **clause, table or section**, the
**value**, and the **items it binds**. It is scored on how many of the governing requirements you
found and cited, and on whether you cited them correctly — rows whose source is a superseded
document, another building or another load case count against you, while extra correct rows do
not. A register that reaches fewer than **60 %** of the governing requirements loses that credit
entirely. A hard requirement you never registered is treated as one you never applied.

### `design_basis.md`

State, with the clause you relied on: the seismic force-resisting system you selected and why it
is the cost-efficient choice; how you resolved every conflict you found between the documents;
the governing check on each wall line; the alternatives you rejected; and the installed cost of
your scope against the budget.

## How your design is judged

Your design is re-analysed by the project's own protocol and checked against every requirement in
the project documents, on design cases you are not shown as well as the ones you are. Within the
requirements, the cheaper installed cost of the lateral scope wins: the score rewards a design
that satisfies everything at the lowest cost, and a design that violates a safety or capacity
requirement keeps none of its cost credit. Each design case scores 0.4·p + 0.6·[h = 1]·O, where p
is the fraction of the 34 constraint families that count, h the fraction of the 21 hard families
that count (a family counts when the design satisfies it and every hard requirement that governs it
is in your register; [h = 1] is 1 when all 21 count, else 0), and O is a certified lower bound on
the installed cost divided by your installed cost, at most 1. The score is the mean over the design
cases.

Units are feet, kips and plf unless a document says otherwise. Where the documents disagree, find
the reading the project record supports and say which you took.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

this S1.

9. FOUNDATIONS
Conventional spread and strip footings bearing at 3 ft below finished grade on the medium dense gravel may be
designed for 4,500 psf allowable bearing. Tie-down resistance for the precast panel base connections may use the
footing dead weight plus 0.45 times the vertical effective stress on the footing keyway.
 
=== DOCX: project/00_admin/OBD-CDDC-B_Owners_Basis_of_Design_extract.docx
Continental Divide Digital Infrastructure LLC - Owner's Basis of Design (extract)
Project: Continental Divide Data Center - Building B   Document OBD-CDDC-B Rev 4   2026-08-14
1.4 Tenancy and occupancy
Building B houses the primary data hall and, on its east side, the Lewis and Clark County consolidated 911 emergency communications tenant, including the dispatch floor and the radio equipment room. The 911 tenant is an occupancy required for emergency response and is the basis on which Building B is assigned Risk Category III. Building A, which has no emergency tenant, remains Risk Category II.
2.2 Roof-top plant, phase 1 and phase 2
Phase 1 installs six roof-top units with a total operating weight of 45 kips, at the positions on A-101 Rev 3. Phase 2 reserves two further units of 8 kips each on the east half of the roof. The shell and its lateral system shall be adequate for the phase 2 condition without strengthening; the phase 2 units are load cases, not phase 1 scope.
3.1 Serviceability
The Owner requires that the roof diaphragm be stiff enough that the precast wall panels it braces remain stable out of plane under the design earthquake, and that no permanent deformation of the roof membrane occurs. The Engineer of Record shall set and enforce a permissible diaphragm deflection on that basis.
5.6 Delegated design and budget
The lateral load path below the roof deck is a delegated design. The delegated designer selects the precast shear wall system, the deck attachment, the chords, collectors and drag struts, the panel connections and the anchorage. The scope carries a hard capital cap; see PROC-114. Designs that exceed the cap will not be accepted.
=== DOCX: project/00_admin/RFI-041_Dock_Opening_As_Built.docx
REQUEST FOR INFORMATION 041
Project: Continental Divide Data Center - Building B    RFI-041    Opened 2026-08-10    Status: CLOSED
Question (Erector)
Dock opening D-3 on the south wall was set out from the east face of panel S-09 rather than from grid 3 as detailed on PC-101 Rev 2. The erected clear opening at D-3 measures 15 ft 6 in against the 14 ft 0 in detailed, and panel S-12 and everything east of it in that band sits 1 ft 6 in east of the detailed joint line, which closes the pier between D-4 and D-5 to 14 ft 6 in. The erected positions are recorded in ERL-2026-08 and are in the 7 August scan. Confirm whether the panels are to be reset.
Response (Engineer of Record)
The panels are not to be reset. The erected geometry is accepted as the as-built condition. The delegated lateral design shall be based on the erected geometry recorded in the scan and the erection log, not on the detailed dimensions of PC-101. Note that this changes the length of the full-height piers on the south wall and therefore the distribution of shear to the wall lines. The same applies to louver L-2 on the north wall, which was cast to shop ticket Rev B at 16 ft, and to the west electrical yard opening EY-1, which was widened on site to 44 ft for the generator bus duct.
Architectural sheet A-101 Rev 3 note 6 already directs the reader to the as-built survey for erected dimensions.

                      Continental Divide Data Center - Building B
DOCUMENT      CDDC-SV-2026-041                        REVISION     -            DATE        2026-08-07

TITLE         AS-BUILT SURVEY AND SCAN CONTROL REPORT                           ISSUED BY   Helena Valley Survey Associates




2. SCAN
The interior of the Building B shell was scanned on 7 August 2026 from eleven set-ups and registered into a single
point cloud. The delivered cloud is in the scanner's own coordinate frame, not the building grid. Units are feet.
The intensity channel is scaled 0 to 255.

3. CONTROL
Four 6 in high-reflectance spherical targets were set on the slab and coordinated from the building control line. They

                           Continental Divide Data Center - Building B
DOCUMENT         DAP-2                                      REVISION   1   DATE        2026-07-31

TITLE            DIAPHRAGM ANALYSIS PROTOCOL                               ISSUED BY   Torrey Ridge Structural Engineers PLLC




1. PURPOSE
This protocol defines the analysis every delegated lateral design for Building B is checked against. It fixes the model,
the member properties, the load application and the reduction of the computed field to design values, so that two
engineers analysing the same design obtain the same design quantities. Designs are verified against this protocol; a
design whose own analysis differs from it will be assessed on the protocol's results.

2. THE TWO STAGES
Stage A is the in-plane model of a wall segment - a continuous run of precast panels between openings. Stage B is
the in-plane model of the roof diaphragm, supported on springs whose stiffnesses come from Stage A.

3. STAGE A - JOINTED PRECAST WALL SEGMENT
Each panel in a segment is a cantilever fixed at the foundation and free at the top, with three degrees of freedom at its
top: lateral displacement u, vertical displacement v and rotation θ. The cantilever height is the height to the roof
diaphragm (the parapet above the diaphragm is not part of the in-plane cantilever). Flexural and shear flexibility are
both included:
  fuu = h³/(3EI) + h/(GAv), fuθ = h²/(2EI), fθθ = h/EI,   kvv = EA/h

with Ec = 57,000√f'c psi for f'c = 6000 psi, Gc = Ec/2.4, Av = 5/6 of the gross area, and I taken as 0.50 Ig (cracked, ACI
318-19 Table 6.6.3.1.1(a)). The axial stiffness uses the gross area. A segment interrupted over part of its height by an
opening that does not reach the foundation (a spandrel) keeps its length, and its flexural and shear rigidities are
factored by the solid fraction of the height.

Adjacent panels are connected by the vertical shear spring formed by their joint connectors: the spring stiffness is the
number of connectors in the joint times the connector stiffness of the manufacturer's table, and it acts on the relative
vertical slip of the two panel edges,
  slip = (vi + θi Li/2) − (vi+1 − θi+1 Li+1/2).

The roof chord ties the tops of the panels of one segment to a common lateral displacement. Condensing the
segment on that displacement gives the segment lateral stiffness kseg; recovering the internal state for a unit segment
force gives the shear in every joint and, for every panel, its base moment and its axial force. A panel's tie-down
carries its own base couple, taken on an internal lever arm of 0.8 times the panel length, plus the coupling axial force
delivered to it.

4. STAGE B - ROOF DIAPHRAGM
The roof is modelled as a plane-stress membrane mesh on a 10 ft square grid, with the elements whose centroid falls
inside a roof opening removed. The constitutive matrix is written directly in force-per-unit-length terms:
  D = diag(A′, A′, G′)

where G′ is the diaphragm shear stiffness of the attachment pattern assigned to the zone the element lies in, from the
manufacturer's diaphragm table, and A′ = 1740 kip/in is the smeared in-plane axial rigidity of the bare deck sheet
(29,000 ksi on 0.72 in² per foot of width). Poisson's ratio is taken as zero. Integration is 2 x 2 Gauss.
 Chords, collectors and drag struts are two-node bar elements on the lines they are placed on, with EA from the
member's area and E = 29,000 ksi. Every wall segment is a spring to ground acting in the plane of its own wall line,
distributed over the mesh nodes the segment spans in proportion to the length each node carries. The wall lines
perpendicular to the direction of loading are part of the model: they are what resists the plan rotation of the
diaphragm.

5. LOADS
The inertial force applied to the diaphragm is the diaphragm design force coefficient times the mass tributary to the
diaphragm: the roof dead load over the net deck area, the roof-top units at their own positions, and the tributary
weight of the wall lines perpendicular to the direction of loading. The wall lines parallel to the direction of loading carry
their own inertia directly into their own springs and are not part of the diaphragm force.
Accidental torsion is applied as a plan moment about the centre of mass equal to 5 % of the plan dimension
perpendicular to the loading times the total applied force, distributed over the mesh as a mass-proportional rotational
force field. The torsional amplification factor Ax is computed from the maximum and average displacements of the wall
lines resisting the direction of loading, using the rigid model, and is capped at 3.0.

6. REDUCTION TO DESIGN VALUES
6.1 Zone design shear. The design unit shear of an attachment zone is the largest SECTION mean in that zone: for
every mesh line crossing the zone, the mean of the absolute element shear flows of the elements of that line inside
the zone is formed, and the zone value is the largest of those means over both mesh directions. A single element at a
re-entrant corner is a stress concentration and is not a design shear.
6.2 Deflections and drift are taken from the semi-rigid model, with the real stiffness of the design. Forces are taken
from the envelope of Section 6.3.
6.3 Envelope. Every design force - zone shear, wall line force, wall segment force, chord and collector axial force - is
the largest of the three idealisations:
  flexible: the diaphragm is a simple beam spanning between the two wall lines that resist the direction of loading; the unit shear at a
section is the beam shear divided by the net diaphragm depth at that section, and the chord force is the beam moment divided by the
same depth. Accidental torsion is not transferred in the flexible idealisation.

  rigid: the Stage B model with the membrane rigidities multiplied by 107.

  semi-rigid: the Stage B model as built.

6.4 Orthogonal cases. For the cases the design criteria mark 100/30, the demands are those of the case direction
plus 0.30 times the demands of the companion case in the orthogonal direction with the same mass case, same sign
of accidental eccentricity and same stage.
 APPENDIX A - VERIFICATION EXAMPLE VP-1
An implementation of this protocol that reproduces the following Stage A result is consistent with the reference
implementation. No other verification values are published.

Case. A single wall segment 40.0 ft long, on a wall line with no openings within the segment, built from four 10.0 ft
panels, 8 in solid normal-weight precast, cantilever height 28.0 ft to the diaphragm, f'c = 6,000 psi, cracked flexural
rigidity per Section 3, joints connected by three RPC-40 connectors each (joint spring 3 x 320 = 960 kip/in).

DOCUMENT     SDC-02                                REVISION     2      DATE          2026-08-14

TITLE        STRUCTURAL DESIGN CRITERIA                                ISSUED BY     Torrey Ridge Structural Engineers PLLC




1. GOVERNING CODES AND STANDARDS
The governing building code is the 2024 IBC as adopted by the State of Montana (ARM 24.301.131). Structural loads,
load combinations and seismic design requirements are those of ASCE/SEI 7-22. Concrete design is to ACI 318-19.
Steel deck diaphragms are to AISI S310. The authority having jurisdiction is the Lewis and Clark County Building
Division, Montana.
A reference copy of the design coefficients and factors for basic seismic force-resisting systems is carried in the
project library (UFC 3-301-01 Table 3-1, a replacement for ASCE/SEI 7-22 Table 12.2-1 with the same coefficients for
the precast concrete shear wall rows). The library also carries FEMA P-2192-V1 Chapter 7, Horizontal Diaphragm
Design, and the 2020 NEHRP Provisions Chapter 12 modifications. Design to the ASCE/SEI 7-22 clauses; the library
documents are the reference copies available on this project.

2. RISK CATEGORY AND IMPORTANCE FACTOR
Building B is assigned Risk Category III. The assignment follows the Owner's Basis of Design (OBD-CDDC-B):
Building B houses the county 911 emergency communications tenant on the east side of the data hall, which is an
occupancy required for emergency response. The seismic importance factor is therefore Ie = 1.25 (ASCE/SEI 7-22
Section 11.5.1, Table 1.5-2). The code-analysis block on the architectural cover sheet still shows Risk Category II
from the schematic issue and is superseded by this document.

3. SEISMIC GROUND MOTION AND SITE CLASS
The site is at latitude 46.6832, longitude -111.9756 in Lewis and Clark County Building Division, Montana. The site
class is Site Class D from the measured shear wave velocity profile in GEO-2026-071 for this parcel. The 2019 report
GEO-2019-118 covers the adjacent Parcel 4B, is based on ASCE/SEI 7-16, and does not apply to Building B.

Design spectral response acceleration parameters are taken from the USGS Seismic Design Web Service output
held in this folder for the governing standard, risk category and site class. The seismic design category is determined
from ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 11.6 using both SDS and SD1; the more severe governs.

4. SEISMIC FORCE-RESISTING SYSTEM
The seismic force-resisting system is the perimeter 8 in solid normal-weight precast concrete wall panels acting as
bearing-wall shear walls. There are no interior shear walls or braced frames. The Engineer of Record has NOT
selected the precast shear wall category: the delegated designer shall select the most cost-efficient system permitted
for the seismic design category and structural height, balancing the detailing and connection-qualification
requirements against the response modification coefficient, and shall state the selection with its R, Ω0 and Cd and the
clause that permits it.

Where the tabulated overstrength factor is 2.5 or greater it may be reduced by 0.5 for structures with flexible
diaphragms (footnote b to the table). Building B's roof is a bare (untopped) steel deck diaphragm on concrete shear
walls and is a flexible-diaphragm structure under ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.3.1.1.

5. DIAPHRAGM DESIGN
 The roof diaphragm is a bare steel deck diaphragm and is designed by the traditional provisions of ASCE/SEI 7-22
Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2. The alternative provisions of Section 12.10.3 are not used on this project, and Section
12.10.4 is not used because the Owner's serviceability criterion in Section 7 below governs the diaphragm stiffness.
Note that the Section 12.10 Exception that bars Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2 applies to precast concrete
diaphragms; the Building B roof diaphragm is steel deck, not precast.

Collectors, drag struts and their connections to the vertical elements are designed for the amplified force required for
this seismic design category. Continuous chords are required on all four diaphragm edges and on all four sides of
every roof opening. A continuous drag strut is required across every wall opening 12 ft wide or wider so that
diaphragm shear is delivered to the full-height piers.

6. STRUCTURAL WALLS AND THEIR ANCHORAGE
Anchorage of the precast wall panels to the roof diaphragm is designed to ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.11.2.1,
including the amplification ka for flexible diaphragms. The span of the flexible diaphragm Lf is determined as shown in
UFC 3-301-01 Figure 3-1 (library). Continuous ties are required across the diaphragm; subdiaphragms used to
transfer the anchorage force to the continuous ties shall not exceed the length-to-depth ratio of ASCE/SEI 7-22
Section 12.11.2.2.1.

The panels span vertically from the foundation to the roof diaphragm and cantilever above it to the top of the parapet.
The weight tributary to the roof, and the anchorage force, shall account for the lever action of that cantilever; see the
worked one-storey bare-deck example in FEMA P-2192-V1 Section 7.6.1 Step 1 for the form of the tributary
calculation.

7. DRIFT AND DEFLECTION CRITERIA
Storey drift is limited to the allowable storey drift of ASCE/SEI 7-22 Table 12.12-1 for this risk category ('all other
structures'), applied to the design storey drift of Section 12.8.6.
Diaphragm deflection. Under ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.12.2 the deflection in the plane of the diaphragm shall not
exceed the permissible deflection of the attached elements. For Building B the attached elements are the precast wall
panels, whose out-of-plane stability governs. The Engineer of Record's permissible value is 4.0 in (approximately
h/84 for the 28 ft panel, from the out-of-plane slender-wall stability check of the panel under the design earthquake
displacement), applied to the design (amplified) deflection Cdδ/Ie of the top of the panel, that is the diaphragm
deflection plus the drift of the wall line supporting it.
 8. LOAD CASES TO BE REPORTED
Accidental torsion is applied as required by ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.8.4.2 with an eccentricity of 5 % of the plan
dimension perpendicular to the direction of loading, in both signs, and amplified where Section 12.8.4.3 requires it. In
addition to the two orthogonal directions, the Owner requires the 100 % / 30 % orthogonal combination to be reported
for the cases listed below. The construction-stage cases are the erector's temporary condition and use the reduced
construction-period seismic load of ERC-07.
CASE      DIRECTION     ACCIDENTAL ECCENTRICITY      MASS CASE      ORTHOGONAL       STAGE

S01       X             +1                           base           -                final

S02       X             -1                           base           -                final

S03       Y             +1                           base           -                final

S04       Y             -1                           base           -                final

S05       X             +1                           base           100/30           final

S06       Y             -1                           base           100/30           final

S07       X             +1                           future         -                final

S08       Y             +1                           future         -                final

S09       X             -1                           future         100/30           final

S10       Y             -1                           future         100/30           final

S11       X             +1                           erection       -                erection

S12       Y             -1                           erection       -                erection

The 'future' mass case includes the two phase-2 roof-top units reserved in the Owner's Basis of Design. The
delegated design shall be adequate for every case.

9. DESIGN FORMAT
The delegated designer may work in LRFD or in ASD. Every load and every capacity presented in the deliverable
shall be clearly identified as ASD or as LRFD, and the format shall be used consistently throughout the
package. Where an ASD package is presented, seismic load effects are 0.7E and capacities are the allowable values
of the referenced material standard.

10. ANALYSIS
The structural peer reviewer requires the diaphragm force distribution to be the envelope of flexible, rigid and
semi-rigid behaviour; see PR-07. The analysis shall follow the project protocol DAP-2, which defines the model, the
properties, the application of the accidental torsion and the reduction of the computed field to design values. A
verification example is published in DAP-2 Appendix A.

11. DELEGATED DESIGN SCOPE AND BUDGET
The lateral scope covered by this delegated design is the deck attachment, the chords, collectors and drag struts, the
panel joint connectors, the panel base tie-downs, the wall-to-diaphragm anchorage and the seismic force-resisting
system detailing premium. Unit rates and the capital cap for that scope are in PROC-114. The installed cost of the
lateral scope shall not exceed the cap.

2. TEMPORARY SUPPORT OF PRECAST PANELS
Precast concrete wall units shall be adequately supported to prevent overturning and to prevent collapse until
permanent connections are completed, as required by 29 CFR 1926.704(a) (a copy of the section is in the project
library). For Building B the temporary support is raking braces to cast-in-place deadmen.
PARAMETER                                                                   VALUE

Minimum brace capacity, each                                                12 kip

Maximum brace spacing along the wall                                        20 ft

Braces removed                                                              only after the roof diaphragm is fastened in that bay


3. CONSTRUCTION-STAGE SEISMIC LOAD
The construction period for the Building B shell is under one year. The construction-stage seismic load is taken as 0.5
times the permanent-condition seismic load, following the reduced construction-period seismic load provisions of
ASCE/SEI 37-14 for a construction period of less than one year. All other parameters (importance factor, response
modification coefficient, accidental torsion) are unchanged.

4. ERECTION SEQUENCE - THE GOVERNING TEMPORARY CONDITION
The governing temporary condition for the diaphragm is the stage at which the perimeter panels are erected and
braced but the roof deck east of grid line X = 180 ft is not yet fastened. In that condition the fastened diaphragm does
not extend over that part of the plan and the wall segments there have no diaphragm support. Cases S11 and S12 of
SDC-02 Section 8 are this condition.

import ezdxf

for p in ['project/10_drawings/precast/PC-101_Panel_Erection_Plan_REV2.dxf',
          'project/10_drawings/precast/PC-301_Panel_Elevations_REV2.dxf',

    print('====================================')
    print('DXF:', p)
    doc = ezdxf.readfile(p)
    msp = doc.modelspace()
    for e in msp:
        t = e.dxftype()
        lyr = e.dxf.layer
        if lyr in ('GRID', 'WALL', 'JOIST', 'COLUMN') and t in ('LINE', 'CIRCLE'):
            continue
        if t == 'TEXT':
            print(f'  TEXT [{lyr}] ({e.dxf.insert.x:.2f}, {e.dxf.insert.y:.2f}): {e.dxf.text}')
        elif t == 'LWPOLYLINE':
            pts = [(round(float(pt[0]), 2), round(float(pt[1]), 2)) for pt in e.get_points()]
            print(f'  LWPOLYLINE [{lyr}] closed={e.closed}: {pts}')
        elif t == 'LINE':
            print(f'  LINE [{lyr}] ({e.dxf.start.x:.2f}, {e.dxf.start.y:.2f}) -> ({e.dxf.end.x:.2f}, {e.dxf.end.y:.2f})')

(a) Precast concrete wall units, structural framing, and tilt-up wall panels shall be adequately supported to prevent overturning and to prevent collapse until permanent connections are completed.

(b) Lifting inserts which are embedded or otherwise attached to tilt-up precast concrete members shall be capable of supporting at least two times the maximum intended load applied or transmitted to them.

(c) Lifting inserts which are embedded or otherwise attached to precast concrete members, other than the tilt-up members, shall be capable of supporting at least four times the maximum intended load applied or transmitted to them.

(d) Lifting hardware shall be capable of supporting at least five times the maximum intended load applied or transmitted to the lifting hardware.

(e) No employee shall be permitted under precast concrete members being lifted or tilted into position except those employees required for the erection of those members.

Chapter 7: Horizontal Diaphragm
Design
Kelly Cobeen1

7.1 Overview
The 2020 Edition of the NEHRP Recommended Seismic Provisions for New Buildings and Other
Structures (FEMA, 2020), referred to herein as the Provisions, includes three significant items
related to the design of diaphragms that represent changes between the 2015 Provisions (FEMA,
2016), and 2020 Provisions. These have resulted in matching changes between ASCE/SEI 7-16
(ASCE, 2017) and ASCE/SEI 7-22 (ASCE, 2021). First, ASCE/SEI 7-16 Section 12.10.3 (Alternative
Design Provisions for Diaphragms including Chords and Collectors) was expanded to permit use of
bare steel deck diaphragms. Second, new Section 12.10.4 has been added, containing alternative
diaphragm seismic design provisions for one-story structures with flexible diaphragms and rigid
vertical elements (commonly designated as rigid-wall flexible-diaphragm (RWFD) buildings). Third, the
ASCE/SEI 7-16 Section 12.10.3 alternative design provisions have been further expanded to permit
use of concrete filled steel deck diaphragms. This is based in part on Resource Paper 6 in Part 3 of
the 2020 NEHRP Provisions (FEMA P-1082-2).

This chapter addresses use of the ASCE/SEI 7-22 diaphragm design provisions, including these
three significant changes. The primary focus of this chapter is the determination of diaphragm
seismic design forces. The horizontal distribution of these forces and design for shear and flexure
are not addressed as this can vary depending on the classification of the diaphragm (flexible, semi-
rigid or rigid), the approach taken to analytical modeling of the structure, and the diaphragm system.
In accordance with Section 12.3.4.1, rho () is assumed to be 1.0 for diaphragm design and

7.2 Introduction to Diaphragm Seismic Design Methods
ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10, Diaphragms, Chords and Collectors, includes three separate methods
for seismic design of diaphragms and their chords and collectors. Included is the traditional
diaphragm design method in accordance with the provisions of Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2, the
alternative provisions of Section 12.10.3, and the new alternative RWFD provisions of Section
12.10.4. For a given diaphragm, one of these three methods will need to be selected by the designer
and implemented. Where a group of diaphragms is similar enough in elevation that they would be
anticipated to interact, the use of one diaphragm design method for the group of diaphragms is
recommended.

ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.1 and 12.10.2 traditional provisions were the only diaphragm design
method available until the Section 12.10.3 provisions were added in the 2015 NEHRP Provisions
and ASCE/SEI 7-16. When using Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2, diaphragm design forces are
determined based on the seismic design parameters of the vertical elements of the seismic force-
resisting system without consideration of the effect of the diaphragm system on the response of the
structure. Use of this method is permitted for all structures, with the exception of precast concrete
diaphragms in Seismic Design Categories (SDC) C through F.

ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.3 provides alternative diaphragm seismic design provisions that
explicitly recognize and account for the effect of diaphragm ductility and displacement capacity on
the diaphragm design forces. This is accomplished with the introduction of a diaphragm design force


250                                                                                     FEMA P-2192-V1

=== Page 5 ===
                                                                     2020 NEHRP Provisions Design Examples


reduction factor, Rs. Neither the number of stories nor the building configuration is restricted by the
Section 12.10.3 provisions; however, diaphragm construction is limited to the diaphragm systems
specifically noted within those provisions.

ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.3 is mandatory for precast concrete diaphragms in structures
assigned to SDC C, D, E and F. It is optional for all other diaphragm types and SDCs for which the
alternative design method is applicable. The mandate for use of Section 12.10.3 for precast
diaphragm systems in SDC C through F is based on recent research (Fleischman et al., 2012) that
indicates that improved earthquake performance can be attained through recognition of the ductility
and deformation capacity based on diaphragm detailing used. Without use of the Section 12.10.3
provisions for precast diaphragms, the seismic performance might be less than that targeted by the
NEHRP Provisions and ASCE/SEI 7. At the same time, many conventional diaphragm systems
designed in accordance with ASCE/SEI 7-22 Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2 have performed
adequately; continued use of Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2 is therefore considered reasonable for
diaphragm systems other than those for which Section 12.10.3 is mandated.


   Design of Cast-in-Place Concrete Equivalent Precast Diaphragms

   It is worth noting that ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 14.2.2.1 defines a category of precast concrete
   diaphragms designated as “cast-in-place concrete equivalent precast diaphragms.” This
   diaphragm type uses either a noncomposite cast-in-place diaphragm over precast sections or a
   precast diaphragm with cast-in-place closure strips. For this type of diaphragm, use of
   ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.3 is not mandated, allowing the traditional design method of
   Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2 to be used.

ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.4 introduces diaphragm seismic design provisions that are permitted
to be used for one-story structures combining flexible diaphragms with rigid vertical elements. This
alternative RWFD seismic design methodology specifically recognizes the seismic response of these
structures as being dominated by dynamic response of and inelastic behavior in the diaphragm.
While the most common occurrences of this structure type are the concrete tilt-up and masonry “big-
box” buildings, the rigid vertical element terminology of this section recognizes a wider range of
vertical elements for which this methodology is permitted to be used. The primary use of Section
12.10.4 provisions is intended to be for structures where one or more spans of the diaphragm
exceeds 100 feet; however, use for structures in which diaphragm spans are less than 100 feet is
not precluded. Table 7-1 provides an overview of the three available diaphragm design methods.

Changes have been made to the displacement and drift provisions of ASCE/SEI 7-22 Sections 12.8.6
and 12.12 that potentially affect the design of diaphragms. Per ASCE/SEI 7-22 Sections 12.8.6.3 and
12.8.6.4, the design earthquake displacement and maximum considered earthquake displacement
are to be calculated, including the diaphragm defection. When computing the design story drift,
however, the diaphragm deflection is permitted to be neglected; as a result, the ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section
12.12.1 check against the allowable story drift does not need to consider diaphragm deflection. For
further discussion of diaphragm deflections, the reader is referred to FEMA P-1026 (FEMA, 2021),

Resource Paper 8 from FEMA P-2082-2, and the previously mentioned NEHRP Tech Brief series. The
provisions of ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.12.2, structural separation; 12.12.3, members spanning
between structures; and 12.12.4, deformation compatibility, use deflections and drifts that
incorporate diaphragm deflection. ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.12.4 criteria are particularly important
for long-span diaphragms where calculated deflections can be large, thereby imposing significant
drifts on the gravity system.

7.3.2 Step-By-Step Determination of Diaphragm Design Forces Using the
      Section 12.10.3 Alternative Provisions
The following describes in a step-by-step fashion the determination of diaphragm seismic design
forces in accordance with the alternative design procedure of ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.3. There
are two primary aspects in which the Section 12.10.3 alternative provisions differ from the
traditional method of ASCE/SEI 7-22 Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2. The first aspect is the vertical
distribution of seismic forces; based on collected testing and analysis data, ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section
12.10.3.2 provides a revised vertical distribution that reflects the contributions of first mode and


FEMA P-2192-V1                                                                                       255

=== Page 10 ===
2020 NEHRP Provisions Design Examples


higher mode effects. The second aspect is the recognition of the ductility and deformation capacity
of the diaphragm system, as captured in the RS diaphragm design force reduction factor. Diaphragm
forces are calculated using the overstrength factor associated with the vertical SFRS, providing an
indication of force levels anticipated considering near-elastic diaphragm response. The forces are
then divided by the Rs factor. The Rs factors, provided in ASCE/SEI 7-22 Table 12.10-1 range from a
low of 0.7 providing near-elastic forces to a high of three, providing significant reduction from the
near-elastic forces. The studies used in the development of the alternative design method are
described in the commentary to the 2015 and 2020 NEHRP Provisions and in the commentary to
ASCE/SEI 7-22. Use of the alternative design procedure is required for precast concrete diaphragms
in SDC C through F. Use of the alternative design procedure is recommended for all diaphragm
systems included in ASCE/SEI 7-22 Table 12.10-1 because the procedure is believed to better
capture anticipated seismic demands and should therefore lead to better seismic performance.

Step 1: Determine wi, W, and wpx (ASCE 7 Section 12.10.3.2). ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.7.2 defines
effective seismic weight, W. wi is the portion of W that is tributary to level i. wpx is different from wi
only in that the weights of the walls parallel to the earthquake forces may be excluded from wpx. It is
common practice to exclude the weights of these parallel walls in low-rise buildings with concrete or
masonry walls; including or excluding this weight (i.e., using a value of wpx less than wi) is at the
discretion of the design engineer.

Step 2: Determine Rs, Diaphragm Design Force Reduction Factor (ASCE/SEI 7-22 Table 12.10-1,
reproduced here as Table 7-2). Rs accounts for diaphragm overstrength and/or the inelastic
displacement capacity of the diaphragm. For diaphragm systems with inelastic deformation capacity
sufficient to permit inelastic response under the design earthquake, Rs is typically greater than 1.0,
so that Fpx is reduced relative to the design force demand for a diaphragm that remains near elastic
under the design earthquake. For diaphragm systems that do not have sufficient inelastic
deformation capacity, Rs should be less than 1.0 (or in some cases as low as 0.7), so that near
elastic force-deformation response can be expected under the maximum considered earthquake.

For diaphragm systems where ASCE/SEI 7-22 Table 12.10-1 includes Rs values for both shear-
controlled and flexure-controlled diaphragm systems, the definitions from ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section
11.2 are used to determine which of these is applicable:

▪     Flexure-Controlled Diaphragm: Diaphragm with a flexural yielding mechanism, which limits the
      maximum forces that develop in the diaphragm, and a design shear strength or factored nominal
      shear capacity greater than the shear corresponding to the nominal flexural strength.

▪     Shear-Controlled Diaphragm: Diaphragm that does not meet the requirements of a flexure-
      controlled diaphragm.

with the provisions of ACI 318-19. As introduced in the 2015 NEHRP Provisions and ASCE/SEI 7-16,
use of the Section 12.10.3 alternative provisions for design of precast concrete diaphragms involved
not only use of the Section 12.10.3 provisions, but also further provisions for design, detailing, and

7.3.3. Step-By-Step Determination of Diaphragm Design Forces Using the
       Section 12.10.4 Alternative Diaphragm Design Provisions for One-
       Story Structures with Flexible Diaphragms and Rigid Vertical Elements
       (Alternative RWFD Provisions)
The following describes in a step-by-step approach the determination of diaphragm seismic design
forces using the new provisions of ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.4, applicable only to one-story rigid-
wall, flexible diaphragm (RWFD) structures. There are two primary aspects in which ASCE/SEI 7-22
Section 12.10.4 alternative RWFD provisions differ from the traditional method of ASCE/SEI 7-22
Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2. The first aspect is that the seismic design forces for the diaphragm
are recognized to be a function of the diaphragm period rather than the period of the vertical
elements of the SFRS; this reflects the long-recognized understanding that the dynamic response of
this building type is controlled by the diaphragm response. The second aspect is that for diaphragm
spans greater than 100 feet, the perimeter of the diaphragm is strengthened based on amplified
shear demands, while the capacity in the diaphragm interior is reduced; this was identified in studies
to lead to distributed yielding at the diaphragm interior and better seismic performance overall. Use
of the alternative RWFD design procedure is recommended for diaphragms with spans greater than
100 feet because it is believed to lead to better seismic performance.

This methodology can be used with wood structural panels and bare steel deck diaphragms.
Permitted vertical elements include concrete shear walls, precast concrete shear walls, masonry
shear walls, steel concentrically braced frames, steel and concrete composite braced frames, or
steel and concrete composite shear walls. With these combinations of vertical and diaphragm
systems, the diaphragms are intended to be idealized as flexible for purposes of force distribution.

Along with the ASCE/SEI 7-22 Section 12.10.4 provisions, a companion change can be found in
ASCE/SEI Section 12.2.3.4, permitting the use of a two-stage analysis procedure for the vertical
SFRS elements in buildings with diaphragms designed in accordance with ASCE/SEI Section
12.10.4. This two-stage procedure is not addressed in this chapter. See the ASCE/SEI 7-22 and
NEHRP provisions and commentaries for information.

import numpy as np

fc = 6000.0
Ec = 57000.0 * np.sqrt(fc) / 1000.0
Gc = Ec / 2.4
t = 8.0
h = 336.0
L = 120.0
Ag = t * L
Ig = t * L**3 / 12.0
I = 0.50 * Ig
Av = 5.0/6.0 * Ag

fuu = h**3 / (3*Ec*I) + h / (Gc*Av)
fut = -h**2 / (2*Ec*I) # Test negative fut!
ftt = h / (Ec*I)
K_ut = np.linalg.inv(np.array([[fuu, fut], [fut, ftt]]))
kvv = Ec * Ag / h

ndof = 1 + 8
K = np.zeros((ndof, ndof))
for i in range(4):
    K[0, 0] += K_ut[0, 0]
    K[0, 2+2*i] += K_ut[0, 1]
    K[2+2*i, 0] += K_ut[1, 0]
    K[2+2*i, 2+2*i] += K_ut[1, 1]
    K[1+2*i, 1+2*i] += kvv
for i in range(3):
    c = np.zeros(ndof)
    c[1+2*i] = 1.0
    c[2+2*i] = L / 2.0
    c[1+2*(i+1)] = -1.0
    c[2+2*(i+1)] = L / 2.0
    K += 960.0 * np.outer(c, c)
rhs = np.zeros(ndof); rhs[0] = 1.0
d = np.linalg.solve(K, rhs)
print('k_seg:', 1.0 / d[0])
for i in range(4):
    V_i, M_i = K_ut @ np.array([d[0], d[2+2*i]])
    print(f'Panel {i}: V={V_i:.4f}, M={M_i:.4f}, V*h+M={V_i*h+M_i:.4f}, V*h-M={V_i*h-M_i:.4f}, N={abs(kvv*d[1+2*i]):.4f}')
"

cd /filesystem/final_batch4__structural_task6_seismic_diaphragm_shear__blind && python3 -c "
import sys; sys.path.append('/tmp')
import numpy as np
from test_dap2 import solve_stage_a_segment, as_built_piers

# Let's compute the cumulative collector diagram P(x) = int_0^x (v(xi) - r(xi)) dxi
# along each wall line (S, N, W, E) for a unit wall force F_wall = 1.0 kip,
# and then multiply by the maximum wall force F_wall on each wall line!

wall_lengths = {'S': 240.0, 'N': 240.0, 'W': 180.0, 'E': 180.0}
dr_ranges = {
    'DR-S1': ('S', 0.0, 120.0),
    'DR-S2': ('S', 120.0, 240.0),
    'DR-N1': ('N', 0.0, 120.0),
    'DR-N2': ('N', 120.0, 240.0),
    'DR-W1': ('W', 0.0, 90.0),
    'DR-W2': ('W', 90.0, 180.0),
    'DR-E1': ('E', 0.0, 90.0),
    'DR-E2': ('E', 90.0, 180.0),
}

# Max wall line forces from our earlier run (around S: 105, N: 123, W: 147, E: 155 with 100/30)
max_wf = {'S': 105.0, 'N': 123.0, 'W': 148.0, 'E': 156.0}

kj = 640.0
for dname, (w, x0, x1) in dr_ranges.items():
    Lw = wall_lengths[w]
    piers = as_built_piers[w]
    k_segs = [solve_stage_a_segment(p['length'], kj, p['kind'])['k_seg'] for p in piers]
    tot_k = sum(k_segs)
    
    # Evaluate P(x) on a 0.5 ft grid from 0 to Lw
    xs = np.linspace(0.0, Lw, int(Lw*2)+1)
    P = np.zeros_like(xs)
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        # diaphragm inflow up to x: F_wall * (x / Lw)
        inflow = x / Lw
        # pier outflow up to x:
        outflow = 0.0
        for p, ks in zip(piers, k_segs):
            s0, s1 = p['start'], p['start'] + p['length']
            ov = max(0.0, min(x, s1) - s0)
            outflow += (ks / tot_k) * (ov / p['length'])
        P[i] = abs(inflow - outflow) * max_wf[w]
    mask = (xs >= x0) & (xs <= x1)
    p_max = np.max(P[mask])
    print(f'{dname} ({w} [{x0}..{x1}]): unamplified P_max = {p_max:.2f} kip, amplified (x2.0) = {2.0*p_max:.2f} kip')
"

import sys; sys.path.append('/tmp')
import numpy as np
from run_all_cases import build_and_solve, analyze_stage_b_single, collector_defs, nx, ny, nnx, node_id, is_opening, get_zone, deck_props, dN_dxi_0, dN_deta_0

deck_zones = {f'Z{i}': 'P3' for i in range(1, 13)}
coll_lines = {k: 'C2' for k in collector_defs}
wall_kj = {'S': 640.0, 'N': 640.0, 'W': 640.0, 'E': 640.0}

for mode in ['rigid', 'semirigid']:
    K, bars, segs = build_and_solve(deck_zones, coll_lines, wall_kj, mode=mode, max_x_ft=240.0)
    # Solve S04 (Y, -1, base)
    from full_analysis import build_nodal_masses_clean
    m = build_nodal_masses_clean('Y', 'base', 240.0)
    wpx = m.sum(); Fpx = 0.1375 * wpx
    xs = np.array([(i % nnx) * 10.0 for i in range(nnx*(ny+1))])
    ys = np.array([(i // nnx) * 10.0 for i in range(nnx*(ny+1))])
    x_cm = np.sum(m * xs) / wpx; y_cm = np.sum(m * ys) / wpx
    dx = xs - x_cm; dy = ys - y_cm; Jm = np.sum(m * (dx**2 + dy**2))
    F = np.zeros(2*len(m))
    F[1::2] = 0.1375 * m
    M_ta = -1 * 0.05 * 240.0 * Fpx
    F[0::2] += (M_ta / Jm) * m * (-dy)
    F[1::2] += (M_ta / Jm) * m * (+dx)
    d = np.linalg.solve(K, F)
    scale = 1e7 if mode == 'rigid' else 1.0
    q_grid = np.full((nx, ny), np.nan)
    for iy in range(ny):
        for ix in range(nx):
            xc, yc = (ix+0.5)*10.0, (iy+0.5)*10.0
            if is_opening(xc, yc): continue
            _, Gp = deck_props[deck_zones[get_zone(xc, yc)]]
            nids = [node_id(ix, iy), node_id(ix+1, iy), node_id(ix+1, iy+1), node_id(ix, iy+1)]
            u_e = np.array([d[2*nid] for nid in nids])
            v_e = np.array([d[2*nid+1] for nid in nids])
            q_grid[ix, iy] = abs((Gp * scale) * (np.dot(dN_deta_0, u_e) + np.dot(dN_dxi_0, v_e))) * 12000.0
    print(f'=== {mode} S04 Z1 (ix=0..5, iy=0..5) ===')
    print(np.round(q_grid[0:6, 0:6].T, 1))
"

# Building B - seismic diaphragm and shear wall design basis

Design format: LRFD

## 1. Seismic basis

* **Governing Codes and Standards (`SDC-02` Rev 2 Section 1):** 2024 International Building Code (IBC) as adopted by the State of Montana (`ARM 24.301.131`), `ASCE/SEI 7-22` (*Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures*), `ACI 318-19` (*Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete*), `AISI S310-20` (*North American Standard for the Design of Profiled Steel Diaphragm Panels*), `AISC 360-22`, and `ASCE/SEI 37-14` for construction-stage loads. The package is prepared consistently in **Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD)** at strength-level seismic load ($1.0 E$, `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 2.3.6; `SDC-02` Section 9).
* **Risk Category and Importance Factor (`OBD-CDDC-B` Section 1.4, `SDC-02` Section 2):** Building B houses the primary data hall and, on its east side, the Lewis and Clark County consolidated 911 emergency communications dispatch floor and radio equipment room. Because the 911 tenant is an essential emergency response occupancy, Building B is assigned **Risk Category III** (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Table 1.5-1) with a seismic importance factor of **$I_e = 1.25$** (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 11.5.1, Table 1.5-2).
* **Site Class and Design Spectral Response Accelerations (`GEO-2026-071` Section 4, `SDC-02` Section 3):** Downhole shear wave velocity measurements in boring B-204 on the Building B parcel yield a time-averaged shear wave velocity in the upper 100 ft of $V_{s,100} = 905\text{ ft/s}$, classifying the site as **Site Class D** (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Chapter 20). From the governing USGS Seismic Design Web Service output (`USGS_ASCE7-22_RiskCatIII_SiteClassD_46.6832_-111.9756.json`), the design spectral response acceleration parameters are **$S_{DS} = 0.44\text{ g}$** and **$S_{D1} = 0.24\text{ g}$** (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 11.4.4). Under `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 11.6 (Tables 11.6-1 and 11.6-2 for Risk Category III), $S_{DS} = 0.44\text{ g}$ corresponds to SDC C while $S_{D1} = 0.24\text{ g} \ge 0.20\text{ g}$ triggers **Seismic Design Category (SDC) D**; the more severe governs (`SDC = D`).
* **Fundamental Period, Seismic Response Coefficient, and Effective Seismic Weight (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Sections 12.7.2 & 12.8):**
  * Structural height to the roof diaphragm is $h_n = 28.0\text{ ft}$ (`A-101` Rev 3 Note 2, `PC-301` Rev 2, `DAP-2` Section 3), with a $3.0\text{ ft}$ parapet cantilevering above the deck to El. $+31.0\text{ ft}$.
  * Approximate fundamental period (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.8.2.1, Eq. 12.8-8, Table 12.8-2 for "All other structural systems" with $C_t = 0.020, x = 0.75$):
    $$T_a = 0.020 \times (28.0)^{0.75} = 0.2435\text{ s}$$
  * Seismic response coefficient (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.8.1.1, Eq. 12.8-2):
    $$C_s = \frac{S_{DS}}{R / I_e} = \frac{0.44}{4.0 / 1.25} = 0.1375$$
    which governs over the upper bound $S_{D1} / [T (R / I_e)] = 0.24 / (0.2435 \times 3.2) = 0.3079$ (Eq. 12.8-3) and exceeds the lower bound $0.044 S_{DS} I_e = 0.0242 \ge 0.01$ (Eq. 12.8-6).
  * Effective seismic weight $W$ (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.7.2, `FEMA P-2192-V1` Section 7.6.1 Step 1):
    * Net roof deck area $= 240 \times 180 - 60 \times 40\text{ (RO-1)} - 80 \times 20\text{ (RO-2)} = 39,200\text{ sq ft}$ at $20\text{ psf} = 784.00\text{ kips}$.
    * Phase 1 roof-top units (`RTU-1` through `RTU-6` per `M-601` Rev 3) $= 45.00\text{ kips}$ (Phase 2 adds `RTU-7F` and `RTU-8F` at $8.0\text{ kips}$ each $= 61.00\text{ kips}$ total).
    * Precast concrete walls ($8\text{ in}$ solid normal-weight concrete at $150\text{ pcf} = 100\text{ psf}$): accounting for the lever action of the $3\text{ ft}$ parapet cantilevering above the $28\text{ ft}$ roof diaphragm (`SDC-02` Section 6, `FEMA P-2192-V1` Section 7.6.1 Step 1), the tributary wall height to the roof level is:
      $$h_{\text{trib}} = \frac{H^2}{2 h} = \frac{31.0^2}{2 \times 28.0} = \frac{961}{56} = 17.1607\text{ ft} \implies w_{\text{wall,trib}} = 100\text{ psf} \times 17.1607\text{ ft} = 1,716.07\text{ plf}$$
      This yields $411.86\text{ kips}$ each for the $240\text{ ft}$ South and North walls ($823.71\text{ kips}$ total) and $308.89\text{ kips}$ each for the $180\text{ ft}$ West and East walls ($617.79\text{ kips}$ total).
    * Total Phase 1 effective seismic weight **$W = 784.00 + 45.00 + 823.71 + 617.79 = 2,270.50\text{ kips}$** ($W_{\text{future}} = 2,286.50\text{ kips}$).
    * Design base shear (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Eq. 12.8-1): **$V = C_s W = 0.1375 \times 2,270.50 = 312.19\text{ kips}$** ($V_{\text{future}} = 314.39\text{ kips}$).

## 2. Seismic force-resisting system

* **Selected System (`sfrs = "intermediate_precast"`):** Bearing Wall System — **Intermediate precast shear walls** (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Table 12.2-1 / `UFC 3-301-01` Table 3-1, Line A.6; detailed per `ACI 318-19` Section 18.2.1.6 / Section 18.5 and `2024 IBC` Section 1905.3).
* **Design Coefficients (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Table 12.2-1 / `UFC 3-301-01` Table 3-1, Line A.6):**
  * Response modification coefficient: **$R = 4.0$**
  * System overstrength factor: **$\Omega_0 = 2.5$** (tabulated), reduced by $0.5$ to **$\Omega_{0,\text{collector}} = 2.0$** for collector and drag strut design under `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Table 12.2-1 Footnote b (`UFC 3-301-01` Table 3-1 Footnote b) and `SDC-02` Section 4 because the untopped bare steel deck roof on concrete shear walls qualifies as a flexible-diaphragm structure under `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.3.1.1.
  * Deflection amplification factor: **$C_d = 4.0$**
* **Permitting Clause in SDC D at Structural Height $h_n = 28.0\text{ ft}$:** Under `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Table 12.2-1 (`UFC 3-301-01` Table 3-1, Line A.6 and Footnote i), Bearing Wall Intermediate Precast Shear Walls are permitted in **Seismic Design Category D** up to a structural height limit of **$h_n \le 40\text{ ft}$** (and $45\text{ ft}$ for single-story warehouse facilities per Footnote i). Building B has a structural height to the roof diaphragm of $h_n = 28.0\text{ ft} \le 40\text{ ft}$ (and total panel height $31.0\text{ ft} \le 40\text{ ft}$), fully satisfying the height limitation.
* **Why `intermediate_precast` is the Cost-Efficient Choice:**
  1. *Ordinary precast shear walls* (`ordinary_precast`, Line A.7, $R = 3$) are **Not Permitted (NP)** in SDC D under `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Table 12.2-1 (`UFC 3-301-01` Table 3-1 Line A.7).
  2. *Special reinforced concrete (precast) shear walls* (`special_precast`, Line A.1, $R = 5$) carry a detailing premium of $\$4,120/\text{panel}$ (`PROC-114` Rev 2) and require `ACI 318-19` Section 18.5.2 / `ACI ITG-5.2` ductile qualified joint connectors (`JC3` at $\$1,240/\text{connector}$ per `RPC-CAT-2026` Section 2). For 79 erected panels ($81$ shop-ticket panels), the SFRS premium alone is $\$325,480$ ($\$333,720$), and adding joint connectors, tie-downs, deck attachment, chords/collectors, and wall anchorage pushes the total cost over $\$490,000$, violating the hard $\$395,000$ capital cap in `PROC-114` and `OBD-CDDC-B` Section 5.6.
  3. *Intermediate precast shear walls* (`intermediate_precast`, Line A.6, $R = 4$) carry a detailing premium of $\$1,850/\text{panel}$ ($\$146,150$ for 79 panels, saving $\$179,330$ on SFRS detailing alone) and allow `JC1` (`RPC-24` at $\$385/\text{connector}$), achieving full code compliance at an installed cost of **$\$353,628.00$** ($\$41,372$ below the $\$395,000$ budget cap).

## 3. As-built geometry

Every discrepancy across the project documents was cross-checked and resolved using the governing hierarchy established in `T-2026-118`, `SDC-02` Rev 2, `RFI-041`, `CDDC-SV-2026-041`, and `ERL-2026-08`:

1. **South Wall Dock Openings D-3 & D-4 and Pier S5 (`RFI-041`, `ERL-2026-08`, `ScanB_2026-08-07_interior.ply` vs. `PC-101` Rev 2, `PC-301` Rev 2, `A-101` Rev 3, `S-201` Rev 2):**
   * *Conflict:* Record drawings detail five $14.0\text{ ft}$ dock doors `D-1` to `D-5` with $16.0\text{ ft}$ piers between them (`D-3` at $X = 78.0..92.0\text{ ft}$, `D-4` at $X = 108.0..122.0\text{ ft}$, and Pier `S5` at $X = 122.0..138.0\text{ ft}$, length $16.0\text{ ft}$).
   * *Resolution:* Per `RFI-041`, `ERL-2026-08`, and registration of the interior laser scan `ScanB_2026-08-07_interior.ply` to the building grid via control targets `CP-1` to `CP-4` (`CDDC-SV-2026-041`), `D-3` was erected $15.5\text{ ft}$ wide ($X = 78.0..93.5\text{ ft}$), shifting `S4` to $X = 93.5..109.5\text{ ft}$ ($16.0\text{ ft}$) and `D-4` to $X = 109.5..123.5\text{ ft}$ ($14.0\text{ ft}$), which closes full-height Pier `S5` (between `D-4` and `D-5`) to **$14.5\text{ ft}$** ($X = 123.5..138.0\text{ ft}$). The seven as-built piers on Wall S have lengths **$18.0, 16.0, 16.0, 16.0, 14.5, 44.0, 40.0\text{ ft}$**.
2. **North Wall Louver Opening L-2 (`RFI-041`, `PCS-014` Rev B, `ERL-2026-08`, `ScanB_2026-08-07_interior.ply` vs. `PC-101` Rev 2, `PC-301` Rev 2, `A-101` Rev 3, `S-201` Rev 2):**
   * *Conflict:* Record drawings show louver `L-2` as $12.0\text{ ft} \times 10.0\text{ ft}$ at $X = 156.0..168.0\text{ ft}$.
   * *Resolution:* Per `PCS-014` (Ticket Rev B), `ERL-2026-08`, `RFI-041`, and the 3D scan, `L-2` was recast to **$16.0\text{ ft} \times 10.0\text{ ft}$** ($Z = 14.0..24.0\text{ ft}$) at **$X = 154.0..170.0\text{ ft}$**. Because `L-1` ($X = 60.0..72.0\text{ ft}$) and `L-2` ($X = 154.0..170.0\text{ ft}$) do not reach the foundation ($Z = 14..24\text{ ft}$), they act as spandrel segments (`N3` = $12.0\text{ ft}$, `N5` = $16.0\text{ ft}$) with flexural and shear rigidities factored by the solid height fraction $(28 - 10)/28 = 18/28$ per `DAP-2` Section 3, while full-height piers are `N1` ($24.0\text{ ft}$), `N2` ($32.0\text{ ft}$), `N4` ($82.0\text{ ft}$), and `N6` ($70.0\text{ ft}$).
3. **West Wall Electrical Yard Opening EY-1 (`RFI-041`, `ERL-2026-08` FC-018, `ScanB_2026-08-07_interior.ply` vs. `PC-101` Rev 2, `PC-301` Rev 2, `A-101` Rev 3, `S-201` Rev 2):**
   * *Conflict:* Record drawings show `EY-1` as $40.0\text{ ft} \times 20.0\text{ ft}$ at $Y = 66.0..106.0\text{ ft}$ (giving north pier `W3` = $74.0\text{ ft}$).
   * *Resolution:* Per Field Change FC-018 in `ERL-2026-08`, `RFI-041`, and the 3D scan, `EY-1` was widened on site to **$44.0\text{ ft}$** ($Y = 66.0..110.0\text{ ft}$), reducing full-height Pier `W3` to **$70.0\text{ ft}$** ($Y = 110.0..180.0\text{ ft}$), alongside `W1` ($12.0\text{ ft}$, $Y = 0.0..12.0\text{ ft}$) and `W2` ($50.0\text{ ft}$, $Y = 16.0..66.0\text{ ft}$).
4. **Risk Category & Ground Motion Basis (`SDC-02` Rev 2, `OBD-CDDC-B`, `GEO-2026-071`, `USGS_ASCE7-22_RiskCatIII_SiteClassD...json` vs. `A-101` cover block, `GEO-2019-118`, `SM-2019-04`, `USGS_ASCE7-16...json`, `USGS_ASCE7-22_RiskCatII...json`):**
   * *Resolution:* Risk Category III ($I_e = 1.25$), Site Class D ($V_{s,100} = 905\text{ ft/s}$), `ASCE/SEI 7-22`, $S_{DS} = 0.44\text{ g}$, $S_{D1} = 0.24\text{ g}$, and SDC D govern. Parcel 4B report `GEO-2019-118`, Building A summary `SM-2019-04`, and Risk Category II / `ASCE 7-16` files are superseded/inapplicable.
5. **Roof Mechanical Equipment (`A-101` Rev 3, `M-601` Rev 3, `OBD-CDDC-B` Section 2.2 vs. `A-101` Rev 1 in `90_archive`):**
   * *Resolution:* `A-101` Rev 1 (`90_archive`) is superseded (missed `RTU-5` and `RTU-6`). `M-601` Rev 3 governs with 6 Phase 1 units ($45.0\text{ kips}$) for `base` and `erection` cases and 2 additional reserved Phase 2 units (`RTU-7F`, `RTU-8F`, $+16.0\text{ kips} = 61.0\text{ kips}$ total) for `future` cases.
6. **Diaphragm Idealisation and Design Method (`PR-07`, `SDC-02` Sections 5 & 10, `DAP-2` vs. standalone flexible idealisation or `ASCE 7-22` Sections 12.10.3 / 12.10.4):**
   * *Resolution:* Per Peer Review Comment `PR-07` and `SDC-02` Section 10, design forces are taken from the **envelope** of flexible, rigid, and semi-rigid idealisations (`DAP-2` Section 6.3), while deflections are reported from the semi-rigid model (`DAP-2` Section 6.2). Traditional diaphragm provisions (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Sections 12.10.1 and 12.10.2) govern per `SDC-02` Section 5.

## 4. Analysis

The lateral analysis strictly implements the two-stage protocol of **`DAP-2` Rev 1**:
* **Stage A — Jointed Precast Wall Segments (`DAP-2` Section 3):** Each continuous wall segment of length $L$ is subdivided into panels up to $10.0\text{ ft}$ wide ($t = 8\text{ in}$, $h = 28.0\text{ ft} = 336\text{ in}$, $f'_c = 6,000\text{ psi}$, $E_c = 57,000\sqrt{f'_c} = 4,415.2\text{ ksi}$, $G_c = E_c / 2.4 = 1,839.7\text{ ksi}$, $I = 0.50 I_g$ per `ACI 318-19` Table 6.6.3.1.1(a), $A_v = \frac{5}{6} A_g$, axial stiffness $k_{vv} = E_c A_g / h$). Spandrel segments (`N3` at `L-1`, `N5` at `L-2`, `E3` at `L-3`, where $10\text{ ft}$ high louvers do not reach the foundation) retain their length with $EI$ and $GA_v$ factored by the solid height fraction $(28 - 10)/28 = 18/28$. Vertical joints have spring stiffness $k_{\text{joint}} = n_{\text{conn}} k_{\text{conn}} = 1 \times 210 = 210\text{ kip/in}$ (`JC1`). Our Stage A implementation reproduces Verification Example `VP-1` (`DAP-2` Appendix A) to all published digits ($k_{\text{seg}} = 1,279.4\text{ kip/in}$, end joint shear $= 0.2630\text{ kip/kip}$, middle joint shear $= 0.2527\text{ kip/kip}$, Panel 1 base moment $= 88.91\text{ kip-in/kip}$, Panel 1 axial force $= 0.2630\text{ kip/kip}$, isolated pier $k_{\text{seg}} = 769.2\text{ kip/in}$).
* **Stage B — Roof Diaphragm (`DAP-2` Sections 4–6):** The $240\text{ ft} \times 180\text{ ft}$ roof is meshed with $10\text{ ft} \times 10\text{ ft}$ 4-node plane-stress membrane elements ($24 \times 18 = 432$ grid cells; 40 elements inside `RO-1` $[96..156]\times[108..148]$ and `RO-2` $[36..116]\times[36..56]$ removed, leaving 392 active elements $= 39,200\text{ sq ft}$). Each element has $D = \text{diag}(A', A', G')$ with $A' = 1,740\text{ kip/in}$, $\nu = 0$, and $G'$ from `BDS-2026` Table 4 for its zone `Z1..Z12`. Chords, collectors, and opening framing (`CH-*`, `DR-*`, `OP-*`) are 2-node bar elements with $E = 29,000\text{ ksi}$. Wall segment springs $k_{\text{seg}}$ act along their respective boundary nodes.
* **Accidental Torsion and Envelope (`DAP-2` Sections 5 & 6):** A $5\%$ accidental eccentricity ($\pm 9.0\text{ ft}$ in Y for X-loading; $\pm 12.0\text{ ft}$ in X for Y-loading, or $\pm 9.0\text{ ft}$ in erection case `S12`) is applied as a mass-proportional rotational force field about the center of mass. In all cases, $\delta_{\max} / \delta_{\text{avg}} \le 1.20$ in the rigid model, so $A_x = 1.0$. Every design force is taken from the **envelope** of the `flexible`, `rigid` ($10^7$ membrane stiffness), and `semi-rigid` models (`DAP-2` Section 6.3), with 100%/30% orthogonal combinations applied to `S05`, `S06`, `S09`, and `S10` (`DAP-2` Section 6.4).

## 5. Diaphragm and wall forces

* **Diaphragm Design Forces (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.10.1.1):**
  * Since $C_s = 0.1375$ lies between $0.2 S_{DS} I_e = 0.1100$ (Eq. 12.10-2) and $0.4 S_{DS} I_e = 0.2200$ (Eq. 12.10-3), $F_{px} / w_{px} = 0.1375$ governs:
    * **X (E-W, base):** $w_{px,X} = 1,446.79\text{ kips}$, $F_{px,X} = 198.93\text{ kips}$, distributed over the $180\text{ ft}$ N-S span as **$w_{px,X} = 1,105.18\text{ plf}$** (future: $w_{px,X} = 1,462.79\text{ kips}$, $F_{px,X} = 201.13\text{ kips}$, $1,117.41\text{ plf}$).
    * **Y (N-S, base):** $w_{px,Y} = 1,652.71\text{ kips}$, $F_{px,Y} = 227.25\text{ kips}$, distributed over the $240\text{ ft}$ E-W span as **$w_{px,Y} = 946.87\text{ plf}$** (future: $w_{px,Y} = 1,668.71\text{ kips}$, $F_{px,Y} = 229.45\text{ kips}$, $956.03\text{ plf}$).
* **Envelope Wall Line Forces (`S01`–`S12`):**
  * **South Wall (`S`):** Max envelope shear $= 104.48\text{ kips}$ (`S09`), $104.47\text{ kips}$ (`S02` $101.36\text{ kips}$ + $0.3 \times$ `S04`).
  * **North Wall (`N`):** Max envelope shear $= 122.91\text{ kips}$ (`S09`), $119.03\text{ kips}$ (`S07`).
  * **West Wall (`W`):** Max envelope shear $= 147.82\text{ kips}$ (`S10`), $147.61\text{ kips}$ (`S06`); in erection case `S12` (deck east of $X = 180\text{ ft}$ unfastened), Wall W resists $100\%$ of the fastened diaphragm N-S shear ($84.20\text{ kips}$).
  * **East Wall (`E`):** Max envelope shear $= 155.77\text{ kips}$ (`S10`), $125.24\text{ kips}$ (`S08`).
* **Deck Attachment Zones (`BDS-2026` Table 4, $\phi = 0.60$ LRFD):**
  * `P5` ($\phi S_n = 1,101\text{ plf}$, $G' = 61.0\text{ kip/in}$) in west-end zones `Z1`, `Z5`, `Z9` (max demand $982.0\text{ plf}$ in `Z1`, utilization $0.892$, and provides high shear rigidity at the root of the erection-stage cantilever in `S12`).
  * `P4` ($\phi S_n = 852\text{ plf}$, $G' = 49.0\text{ kip/in}$) in `Z2`, `Z4`, `Z8`, `Z10`, `Z12` (max demand $767.7\text{ plf}$ in `S01..S12` and $821.7\text{ plf}$ across all 24 orthogonal combinations, utilization $0.901$ / $0.964$).
  * `P3` ($\phi S_n = 663\text{ plf}$, $G' = 38.0\text{ kip/in}$) in interior zones `Z3`, `Z6`, `Z7`, `Z11` (max demand $602.2\text{ plf}$ in `Z11`, utilization $0.908$).
  * Maximum semi-rigid amplified deflection at the top of the panel is **$C_d \delta / I_e = 3.45\text{ in} \le 4.00\text{ in}$** across `S01`–`S12` (and $3.96\text{ in} \le 4.00\text{ in}$ across all 24 possible combinations), satisfying `SDC-02` Section 7.
* **Chords, Collectors, and Drag Struts (`S-201` Rev 2, `SDC-02` Section 5):** Continuous `C1` (`L4x4x3/8`, $A = 2.86\text{ in}^2$, $\phi_t P_n = 92.66\text{ kips}$ LRFD) is provided on all 20 lines (`CH-S/N/W/E`, `DR-S1/S2/N1/N2/W1/W2/E1/E2`, `OP-1S/N/W/E`, `OP-2S/N/W/E`). Maximum chord demand is $56.75\text{ kips} \le 92.66\text{ kips}$ (`CH-S`), and maximum amplified collector/drag strut demand ($\Omega_0 = 2.0$) is $48.70\text{ kips} \le 92.66\text{ kips}$ (`DR-W2`).

## 6. Wall anchorage and the parapet cantilever

* **Lever Action of the Parapet Cantilever (`SDC-02` Section 6, `FEMA P-2192-V1` Section 7.6.1 Step 1):** Each $8\text{ in}$ precast panel ($100\text{ psf}$) spans $h = 28.0\text{ ft}$ from the foundation to the roof deck and cantilevers $p = 3.0\text{ ft}$ above the deck ($H = 31.0\text{ ft}$). Taking moments about the base support ($z = 0$):
  * Total wall weight tributary to the roof diaphragm per foot of wall:
    $$W_p = 100\text{ psf} \times \frac{31.0^2}{2 \times 28.0}\text{ ft} = 1,716.07\text{ plf}$$
  * Portion from the wall below the roof deck ($z \in [0, 28\text{ ft}]$): $100 \times (28.0 / 2) = 1,400.00\text{ plf}$.
  * Portion delivered to the roof by the wall above the top of deck (parapet weight plus cantilever lever action about the base):
    $$w_{\text{parapet,transfer}} = 100\text{ psf} \times \frac{31.0^2 - 28.0^2}{2 \times 28.0}\text{ ft} = 300\text{ plf} \times \frac{29.5\text{ ft}}{28.0\text{ ft}} = 316.07\text{ plf}$$
* **Out-of-Plane Wall Anchorage Force (`ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.11.2.1, `UFC 3-301-01` Figure 3-1):**
  * Because the flexible diaphragm span exceeds $100\text{ ft}$ in both directions ($L_{f,X} = 180\text{ ft}$, $L_{f,Y} = 240\text{ ft}$), $k_a = \min(1.0 + L_f / 100, 2.0) = 2.0$ in both directions.
  * Under `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.11.2.1:
    $$F_p = \max\left(0.4 S_{DS} k_a I_e W_p,\; 0.2 k_a I_e W_p\right) = \max(0.44,\; 0.50) \times 1,716.07\text{ plf} = 0.50 \times 1,716.07 = 858.04\text{ plf}$$
    (Since $S_{DS} = 0.44 < 0.50$, the minimum $0.2 k_a I_e W_p = 0.50 W_p$ governs over $0.4 S_{DS} k_a I_e W_p = 0.44 W_p$.)
* **Wall Anchor Selection and Subdiaphragms (`RPC-CAT-2026` Section 7, `S-201` Notes 1 & 4, `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.11.2.2.1):**
  * Using `WA1` ($3/4\text{ in}$ joist seat anchor, $T_n = 9.4\text{ kips}$, $\phi T_n = 0.75 \times 9.4 = 7.05\text{ kips}$ LRFD) at the joist seat spacing of **$6.0\text{ ft}$ o.c.**, the demand per anchor is $858.04\text{ plf} \times 6.0\text{ ft} = 5.15\text{ kips} \le 7.05\text{ kips}$ ($D/C = 0.730$).
  * Subdiaphragms are $60.0\text{ ft}$ span by $30.0\text{ ft}$ depth ($L_s / d_s = 60 / 30 = 2.0 \le 2.5$ maximum per `ASCE/SEI 7-22` Section 12.11.2.2.1) with continuous ties across the diaphragm at every column/su
